title: State and Command
scopeHtml: Scope: State machines and Command with undo/redo, refactors, Java and Kotlin, real examples.

notes.title: State: the idea
notes.html:
The State pattern lets an object change its behaviour when its internal state changes, by delegating to a separate object per state. Instead of if (state == X) in every method, each state is a class that knows what each action means in that state.

Use it when an object has a handful of modes and the same method behaves differently per mode: vending machine, order lifecycle, media player, TCP connection, document (draft, review, published).

Before (flag + if chain in every method):

class Player {
    enum S { STOPPED, PLAYING, PAUSED }
    S s = S.STOPPED;
    void pressPlay() {
        if (s == S.STOPPED) { start(); s = S.PLAYING; }
        else if (s == S.PLAYING) { pause(); s = S.PAUSED; }
        else if (s == S.PAUSED) { resume(); s = S.PLAYING; }
    }
    void pressStop() { if (s != S.STOPPED) { halt(); s = S.STOPPED; } }
}

With 3 states and 5 actions you can have up to 15 branches spread over methods. Add a "Buffering" state and you edit every method.

After:

interface PlayerState {
    void play(Player p); void stop(Player p);
}
class Stopped implements PlayerState {
    public void play(Player p) { p.startAudio(); p.setState(new Playing()); }
    public void stop(Player p) { /* already stopped: ignore */ }
}
class Playing implements PlayerState {
    public void play(Player p) { p.pauseAudio(); p.setState(new Paused()); }
    public void stop(Player p) { p.haltAudio(); p.setState(new Stopped()); }
}
class Paused implements PlayerState {
    public void play(Player p) { p.resumeAudio(); p.setState(new Playing()); }
    public void stop(Player p) { p.haltAudio(); p.setState(new Stopped()); }
}
class Player {
    private PlayerState state = new Stopped();
    void setState(PlayerState s) { state = s; }
    void pressPlay() { state.play(this); }
    void pressStop() { state.stop(this); }
}
+------------+  state   +-----------------+
| Player     |--------->| <<interface>>   |
| + pressPlay|          | PlayerState     |
| + pressStop|          | play(), stop()  |
+------------+          +--------+--------+
                                 ^
                    +------------+-----------+
                 Stopped      Playing       Paused

Kotlin variant (sealed class, compiler checks every state is handled):

sealed interface PlayerState {
    object Stopped : PlayerState
    object Playing : PlayerState
    object Paused : PlayerState
}
class Player {
    var state: PlayerState = PlayerState.Stopped; private set
    fun onPlay() { state = when (state) {
        PlayerState.Stopped -> PlayerState.Playing
        PlayerState.Playing -> PlayerState.Paused
        PlayerState.Paused  -> PlayerState.Playing
    } }
}

Two valid styles: state-as-object (behaviour inside state classes) and state-as-data with a when (transitions in one function). Kotlin favours the second for small machines.

Decision gravity. Choosing State is a moderate refactor, reversible. The one-way door is persisting states: once "PAID", "SHIPPED" are stored in a DB column, renaming or splitting states needs a data migration.

Everyday analogy. A traffic light: pressing the pedestrian button means something different on red, green and amber.

Common interview traps.

  • Not drawing the transition table. Say states, events, and what is illegal.
  • Allocating a new state object on each transition; stateless states can be singletons (Kotlin object).
  • Letting every state touch every field; the context should expose a small API.

notes.title: Finite state machines in practice
notes.html:
A finite state machine (FSM) is a set of states, a set of events, and a transition table: (current state, event) -> (next state, action). It makes illegal transitions impossible by construction, which is the real value.

Order state machine
                 pay            ship            deliver
   CREATED ------------> PAID ----------> SHIPPED --------> DELIVERED
      |                    |                  |
      | cancel             | refund           | (no cancel here)
      v                    v
  CANCELLED            REFUNDED

Worked example (table-driven). 5 states x 4 events = 20 cells. Only 6 are legal. A table makes that explicit:

enum OrderState { CREATED, PAID, SHIPPED, DELIVERED, CANCELLED, REFUNDED }
enum Event { PAY, SHIP, DELIVER, CANCEL, REFUND }

class OrderFsm {
    private static final Map<OrderState, Map<Event, OrderState>> T = Map.of(
        OrderState.CREATED, Map.of(Event.PAY, OrderState.PAID, Event.CANCEL, OrderState.CANCELLED),
        OrderState.PAID,    Map.of(Event.SHIP, OrderState.SHIPPED, Event.REFUND, OrderState.REFUNDED),
        OrderState.SHIPPED, Map.of(Event.DELIVER, OrderState.DELIVERED));
    OrderState next(OrderState s, Event e) {
        OrderState n = T.getOrDefault(s, Map.of()).get(e);
        if (n == null) throw new IllegalStateException(s + " + " + e);
        return n;
    }
}
val table = mapOf(
    (Created to Pay) to Paid, (Created to Cancel) to Cancelled,
    (Paid to Ship) to Shipped, (Paid to Refund) to Refunded,
    (Shipped to Deliver) to Delivered)
fun next(s: OrderState, e: Event) = table[s to e] ?: error("illegal $s + $e")

Real FSMs. Android: Activity lifecycle, MediaPlayer states (Idle, Initialized, Prepared, Started, Paused, Stopped, End; calling start() in the wrong state throws IllegalStateException), WorkManager.State (ENQUEUED, RUNNING, SUCCEEDED, FAILED, CANCELLED, BLOCKED). Backend: TCP (LISTEN, SYN_RECEIVED, ESTABLISHED, FIN_WAIT, TIME_WAIT ...), Stripe PaymentIntent statuses, AWS Step Functions, Kubernetes pod phases. Libraries: Spring Statemachine, Android StateMachine (internal), Kotlin libs such as Tinder StateMachine.

Production incident pattern. Two concurrent requests both read an order in PAID and both ship it, double-shipping. Symptom: duplicate shipment IDs, state log shows two PAID -> SHIPPED rows. Fix: do the transition atomically, UPDATE orders SET state='SHIPPED' WHERE id=? AND state='PAID' and check affected rows = 1 (optimistic guard), or use a version column.

Decision gravity. A transition table is cheap to write and expensive to change once other services depend on the state names. Add states rarely; prefer adding a sub-state or a flag over splitting a published state.

Everyday analogy. A board game: each square allows only certain moves; the rulebook is the transition table.

Common interview traps.

  • Concurrency: reading state then writing without a guard.
  • Forgetting a terminal state and an error/timeout transition.
  • Letting any code set the state field directly; funnel everything through next.

notes.title: When NOT to use State
notes.html:
• Two states (on/off): a boolean is enough.
  • State affects one method only: a when in that method is simpler than classes.
  • States differ in data, not behaviour: use an enum with fields.
  • Transitions are driven by a huge external workflow (approvals across weeks, multiple actors): use a workflow engine (Temporal, Camunda, Step Functions) instead of hand-rolled classes.

State vs Strategy (the classic confusion): structure is nearly identical (context + interface + implementations). Strategy: the client chooses the algorithm and it rarely changes by itself. State: the object itself swaps its state object when events occur, and states know about each other (Stopped creates Playing).

Cost. One class per state in Java (5 states = 5 files plus interface). Transitions are scattered across classes, so one cannot see the whole graph in one place; a table or a diagram in docs fixes that.

Everyday analogy. A strategy is choosing a route; a state is the car being in gear 1, 2 or reverse (the same pedal does different things).

Common interview traps.

  • Saying "State = Strategy". Explain who triggers the change.
  • Using State when a simple enum + when is more readable.

notes.title: Command: the idea
notes.html:
Command turns a request into an object. Instead of calling light.on() directly, you create TurnOnCommand(light) that carries what to do, on what, with what arguments. Because it is an object you can queue it, log it, schedule it, send it over a network, and undo it.

Roles: Command (interface with execute()), Receiver (does the real work), Invoker (button, queue, scheduler), Client (wires them).

+---------+ executes +-------------+ calls +-----------+
| Invoker |--------->| <<interface>>|------>| Receiver  |
| (button)|          | Command      |       | (Light)   |
+---------+          | execute()    |       +-----------+
                     | undo()       |
                     +------+-------+
                            ^
                 +----------+----------+
            TurnOnCmd          TurnOffCmd

Before: a remote with hard-coded buttons.

class Remote {
    Light light; Fan fan;
    void button1() { light.on(); }
    void button2() { fan.start(); }   // rewiring needs code changes
}

After:

interface Command { void execute(); void undo(); }

class LightOn implements Command {
    private final Light light;
    LightOn(Light l) { light = l; }
    public void execute() { light.on(); }
    public void undo()    { light.off(); }
}
class Remote {
    private Command[] slots = new Command[5];
    void set(int i, Command c) { slots[i] = c; }
    void press(int i) { slots[i].execute(); }
}

Kotlin variant. Without undo, a command is just () -> Unit:

val queue = ArrayDeque<() -> Unit>()
queue += { light.on() }
queue += { fan.start() }
while (queue.isNotEmpty()) queue.removeFirst()()

Real examples. Runnable and Callable (a command with no undo), ExecutorService.submit; Android Handler.post(Runnable), WorkManager Worker (persisted command with retries), Intent + PendingIntent (a command handed to another process to run later); database transaction logs and write-ahead logs (commands replayed on recovery); Redux/MVI actions; job queues like Sidekiq/Celery tasks; Kafka messages used as commands.

Decision gravity. Making requests objects is a modest cost and a flexible door. The one-way part is serialising commands (persisted queues, event sourcing): old command shapes must stay readable forever.

Everyday analogy. A restaurant order slip: the waiter writes it down; the kitchen cooks later, in order; the slip can be cancelled or reprinted.

Common interview traps.

  • Mixing Command with Strategy: Command packages a request (what to do, to whom, with what); Strategy packages an algorithm.
  • Forgetting commands may fail; queued commands need retry/idempotency.
  • Executing a command twice by accident (non-idempotent commands in a retry queue).

notes.title: Undo and redo with Command
notes.html:
Undo works by storing, for each command, enough information to reverse it, and keeping a history stack. Two stacks: undoStack and redoStack.

Algorithm:

  1. execute(cmd): run it, push to undoStack, clear redoStack.
  2. undo(): pop from undoStack, call cmd.undo(), push to redoStack.
  3. redo(): pop from redoStack, call cmd.execute(), push to undoStack.

Worked example (text editor). Document "Hello". Type " World" (cmd1: insert at 5, text " World"), then delete 3 chars (cmd2: delete range 8..11, saved text "rld"). Stack: [cmd1, cmd2]. Undo pops cmd2 and re-inserts "rld" -> "Hello World". Undo again pops cmd1 and deletes " World" -> "Hello". Redo re-applies cmd1. Memory: storing deltas (a few bytes each) rather than a full copy of the document: 10,000 edits x about 50 bytes = 500 KB, versus 10,000 x 100 KB = 1 GB if you snapshot each time.

class History {
    private final Deque<Command> undo = new ArrayDeque<>(), redo = new ArrayDeque<>();
    void run(Command c) { c.execute(); undo.push(c); redo.clear(); }
    void undo() { if (!undo.isEmpty()) { Command c = undo.pop(); c.undo(); redo.push(c); } }
    void redo() { if (!redo.isEmpty()) { Command c = redo.pop(); c.execute(); undo.push(c); } }
}

class InsertText implements Command {
    private final StringBuilder doc; private final int pos; private final String text;
    InsertText(StringBuilder d, int p, String t) { doc = d; pos = p; text = t; }
    public void execute() { doc.insert(pos, text); }
    public void undo()    { doc.delete(pos, pos + text.length()); }
}
class History {
    private val undo = ArrayDeque<Command>(); private val redo = ArrayDeque<Command>()
    fun run(c: Command) { c.execute(); undo.addLast(c); redo.clear() }
    fun undo() { undo.removeLastOrNull()?.also { it.undo(); redo.addLast(it) } }
    fun redo() { redo.removeLastOrNull()?.also { it.execute(); undo.addLast(it) } }
}

Two strategies for undo.

  • Inverse command (above): small, fast, but each command needs a correct inverse. Not every action is reversible (send email, charge card).
  • Memento / snapshot (next notes): store prior state; simple but memory-heavy. Photoshop-style apps use a hybrid (deltas plus periodic snapshots).

Extras for seniors. Macro command = composite of commands (undo reverses in reverse order). Merge consecutive keystrokes into one command so Ctrl+Z undoes a word, not a letter. Cap the stack (for example 100 entries) to bound memory. In collaborative editors (Google Docs), undo must be per-user and transformed against others' edits (Operational Transform or CRDTs).

When NOT to use Command.

  • A single direct method call with no queue, log or undo: just call it.
  • Side effects that cannot be reversed: model compensating actions (refund) instead of pretending to undo.
  • Very hot paths: an object per call adds allocation; lambdas help.

Decision gravity. Choose undo-by-inverse when actions are small and reversible; choose snapshots when state is small or inverses are hard. Switching later is a rewrite of every command, so decide early for editors.

Everyday analogy. A pencil with an eraser, plus a notebook of every stroke you made so you can erase them in reverse order.

Common interview traps.

  • Not clearing the redo stack on a new action.
  • Undoing a command whose receiver state has changed since (the stored position is stale).
  • Unbounded history causing OutOfMemoryError.

notes.title: Summary
notes.html:
• State: an object swaps behaviour by delegating to a state object; removes per-method if chains. Kotlin: sealed interface + when for small machines.
  • FSM: states + events + transition table makes illegal moves impossible. Guard transitions atomically in DB (WHERE state='PAID') to avoid double-processing.
  • State vs Strategy: State changes itself via events; Strategy is chosen by the client. Do not use State for two modes or one varying method.
  • Command: a request as an object (Invoker, Command, Receiver) enabling queues, logs, scheduling, retries. Runnable, Handler.post, WorkManager are examples.
  • Undo/redo: two stacks; undo pops and reverses, new action clears redo. Store deltas or inverses, cap the stack, merge keystrokes.
  • Irreversible actions need compensating commands, not undo; persisted commands need stable schemas.

questions.promptHtml: What is the State pattern and what smell does it remove?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Tests whether you can replace status-flag conditionals with polymorphism.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: An object's behaviour depends on its current state. Instead of if (status == X) in every method, each state is a class that implements the behaviour, and the context delegates to its current state object. Transitions swap that object. It kills the repeated switch over a status field.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Context holds state; the state interface has the actions (pay, ship, cancel). Illegal actions are handled inside each state (throw or ignore), so rules live next to the state they belong to. Who triggers the transition: the state itself (it knows what comes next) or the context.

Order --has-a--> <<OrderState>> <|-- Created --pay--> Paid --ship--> Shipped

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
Languages: Java, Kotlin

Languages: Java · Kotlin
interface OrderState { OrderState pay(); OrderState ship(); OrderState cancel(); }
enum Created implements OrderState {
    INSTANCE;
    public OrderState pay() { return Paid.INSTANCE; }
    public OrderState ship() { throw new IllegalStateException("unpaid"); }
    public OrderState cancel() { return Cancelled.INSTANCE; }
}
sealed interface OrderState {
    fun pay(): OrderState = throw IllegalStateException("cannot pay in $this")
    fun ship(): OrderState = throw IllegalStateException("cannot ship in $this")
    object Created : OrderState { override fun pay() = Paid }
    object Paid : OrderState { override fun ship() = Shipped }
    object Shipped : OrderState
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Keeping both a status enum and a state object, so they drift.
  • Stateful state objects shared as singletons across contexts.
  • A state hierarchy for 2 states.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Who owns transitions? -> States return the next state (decentralised), or a table owns them (centralised).
  2. Can states be singletons? -> Yes if they hold no per-context data.
  3. Persisting state? -> Store an id or enum name; rebuild the object on load.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Senior adds persistence, illegal-transition policy, and when a transition table is simpler.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: Order lifecycles with if status in 15 places produced "shipped but unpaid" orders.

questions.promptHtml: What is the Command pattern and why would you wrap a request in an object?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Core behavioural pattern; checks that you know the benefits beyond "an object with execute".

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Command turns a request into an object with execute(). Because it is an object I can queue it, log it, retry it, schedule it, pass it around and undo it. The invoker does not know what the command does; the receiver does the work.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html: Roles: Command, ConcreteCommand (holds the receiver and parameters), Receiver, Invoker, Client. Real examples: Runnable handed to an executor, Android Handler.post, a job queue, menu actions, WorkManager requests.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
Languages: Java, Kotlin

Languages: Java · Kotlin
interface Command { void execute(); }
class SaveCommand implements Command {
    private final Doc doc;
    SaveCommand(Doc d) { this.doc = d; }
    public void execute() { doc.save(); }
}
class Invoker { void run(Command c) { c.execute(); } }
fun interface Command { fun execute() }
class SaveCommand(private val doc: Doc) : Command { override fun execute() = doc.save() }
val queue = ArrayDeque<Command>()

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Commands that capture mutable shared state and run later with stale data.
  • Using Command for a single synchronous call with no queue, log or undo.
  • Non-serialisable commands when you need persistence.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Command vs Strategy? -> Strategy is how to do something; Command is a request to do it, with parameters and lifecycle.
  2. What do queues add? -> Retry, ordering, rate limiting, persistence.
  3. Is Runnable a Command? -> Yes, a no-undo one.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Senior lists the second-order benefits (logging, retry, undo) and the capture/staleness risk.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A payment retry queue built from serialisable commands survived app restarts.

questions.promptHtml: State and Strategy have the same class diagram. How do you tell them apart?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Intent versus structure; common confusion.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: The structure is identical: a context delegating to an interface. The difference is who changes the object and why. With Strategy the client picks the algorithm and it rarely changes. With State the object changes its own state object as events happen, and states often know about each other (transitions).

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Aspect Strategy State
Who switches client / config the state or context itself
Changes at runtime occasionally constantly, by events
Variants aware of each other no yes (transitions)
Question answered how do we compute this what can we do now

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Calling any interface delegation "State".
  • Using State for purely static configuration choice.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Can a state use a strategy? -> Yes, e.g. a Retrying state using a backoff policy.
  2. Which is more likely to leak invalid transitions? -> State, which is why you centralise or test transitions.
  3. Is a media player a State or Strategy? -> State (play, pause, stop transitions).

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Senior answers by intent and transition ownership, not the diagram.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A connection manager modelled as Strategy kept needing flags; as State it became 4 small classes.

questions.promptHtml: How do you implement undo/redo with Command? Compare storing an inverse versus a snapshot.

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Tests two-stack design and memento trade-offs.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Each command has execute() and undo(). An undo stack holds executed commands; undo pops, calls undo(), and pushes to a redo stack; a new action clears the redo stack. For undo either store the inverse operation (compact) or a memento snapshot of prior state (simple, larger).

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Approach Pros Cons
Inverse operation small memory must be exactly invertible
Memento / snapshot always correct memory heavy; use diffs
Command + captured before-value middle ground store old value per command

Key rules: a new command clears redo; undo must be idempotent-safe; bound the history; group typed characters into one command (coalescing).

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
Languages: Java, Kotlin

Languages: Java · Kotlin
interface Cmd { void execute(); void undo(); }
class History {
    private final Deque<Cmd> undo = new ArrayDeque<>(), redo = new ArrayDeque<>();
    void run(Cmd c) { c.execute(); undo.push(c); redo.clear(); }
    void undo() { if (!undo.isEmpty()) { Cmd c = undo.pop(); c.undo(); redo.push(c); } }
    void redo() { if (!redo.isEmpty()) { Cmd c = redo.pop(); c.execute(); undo.push(c); } }
}
interface Cmd { fun execute(); fun undo() }
class History {
    private val undo = ArrayDeque<Cmd>(); private val redo = ArrayDeque<Cmd>()
    fun run(c: Cmd) { c.execute(); undo.addLast(c); redo.clear() }
    fun undo() { undo.removeLastOrNull()?.also { it.undo(); redo.addLast(it) } }
    fun redo() { redo.removeLastOrNull()?.also { it.execute(); undo.addLast(it) } }
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Not clearing redo on a new command.
  • Undo of a non-invertible action (send email) without compensating logic.
  • Unbounded history.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Delete a character, undo: what is stored? -> Position and the removed character.
  2. Memory control? -> Cap the stack, snapshot diffs, coalesce.
  3. Undo of side effects? -> Compensating commands; or mark non-undoable and flush history.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Senior adds coalescing, bounded history and non-undoable actions.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: An image editor stored full bitmaps per step and OOMed at 30 edits; deltas fixed it.

questions.contextHtml:
Order has String status and four methods, each with a switch over six statuses. Last month cancel() was patched but refund() was not, and a shipped order was refunded twice.

void cancel() {
    switch (status) {
        case "CREATED": status = "CANCELLED"; break;
        case "PAID": refund(); status = "CANCELLED"; break;
        case "SHIPPED": throw new IllegalStateException();
        // 3 more cases
    }
}
questions.promptHtml: Refactor and explain what changes when "On Hold" is added.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Extract each case body to private methods; the status switches remain.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Are transitions only these? Is status persisted as a string (migration impact)? Who calls these methods?
  2. Immediate mitigation: add a test matrix state x action to pin current behaviour, including the double refund.
  3. Approach: one class per state implementing OrderState; Order delegates; keep persisted string as the id.

Languages: Java, Kotlin

Languages: Java · Kotlin
class Order {
    private OrderState state = new Created();
    void cancel() { state = state.cancel(this); }
}
class Paid implements OrderState {
    public OrderState cancel(Order o) { o.refund(); return new Cancelled(); }
    public OrderState ship(Order o) { return new Shipped(); }
}
class Order {
    var state: OrderState = OrderState.Created
    fun cancel() { state = state.cancel(this) }
}
  1. Fix of the bug class: every state must define every action, and the default is "illegal" - the compiler or a base class forces the decision, so a missed case is impossible.
  2. Adding On Hold: one new class plus edits in the states that can enter or leave it (e.g. Paid.hold). Existing unrelated states stay untouched.
  3. Prevention: table-driven test over all state x action pairs.
  4. Trade-offs: six classes for six states; if actions are few and states static, a transition table (enum + map) is less code.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Persist/restore? -> Map stored string to state with a factory; unknown string fails loudly.
  • Audit trail? -> Record every transition in one place.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A patched cancel path left refund open; the state-per-class rewrite made the missing case a compile error.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: private methods only.
  • Hire: State classes with delegation.
  • Strong hire: forced coverage, migration, test matrix, table alternative.

questions.contextHtml:
A vending-machine class allows free drinks: support reports a drink dispensed with no payment after a user pressed "refund" then "select" quickly. Code:

enum S { IDLE, HAS_MONEY, DISPENSING }
S s = S.IDLE;
void insertCoin()  { s = S.HAS_MONEY; }
void refund()      { giveBackCoins(); /* forgot: s = S.IDLE */ }
void select()      { if (s == S.HAS_MONEY) { s = S.DISPENSING; dispense(); s = S.IDLE; } }
questions.promptHtml: Find the bug and describe a design that makes this class of bug hard.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Add s = IDLE and move on; no structural fix or test.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Can events overlap (two button presses)? Is hardware callback threaded?
  2. Immediate mitigation: reset state in refund.
  3. Root cause: a transition was implicit and forgotten; state and side effect (coins returned) disagree.
  4. Fix: make transitions explicit and total: one transition(state, event) table, every pair defined, otherwise throws.

Languages: Java, Kotlin

Languages: Java · Kotlin
S on(S s, Event e) {
    return switch (s) {
        case IDLE -> e == Event.COIN ? S.HAS_MONEY : S.IDLE;
        case HAS_MONEY -> switch (e) { case REFUND -> S.IDLE; case SELECT -> S.DISPENSING; default -> s; };
        case DISPENSING -> s;
    };
}
fun on(s: S, e: Event): S = when (s) {
    S.IDLE -> if (e == Event.COIN) S.HAS_MONEY else S.IDLE
    S.HAS_MONEY -> when (e) { Event.REFUND -> S.IDLE; Event.SELECT -> S.DISPENSING; else -> s }
    S.DISPENSING -> s
}
  1. Concurrency: make on synchronized or serialise events through one queue.
  2. Prevention: exhaustive when/switch (no default), property test: "dispense only after payment".
  3. Trade-offs: a pure transition function plus side-effect executor is testable but adds a layer.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Two presses at once? -> Single-threaded event loop.
  • Payment fails mid-dispense? -> Add a Failed state and refund transition.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A kiosk gave free items when a rarely-used cancel path skipped the reset; a pure transition function with a invariants test closed it.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: one-line fix.
  • Hire: explicit transition table.
  • Strong hire: totality, concurrency, invariant test.

questions.contextHtml: A video upload has states Queued, Uploading, Done, Failed with State classes. Product wants Paused (user taps pause), resumable from the byte offset, and auto-pause when the network drops.
questions.promptHtml: What changes and what does not? What new risks appear?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Add a paused boolean to Uploading.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Can Paused go to Failed? Does auto-pause resume automatically? Is offset persisted across app restarts?
  2. Changes: new Paused state holding the offset; Uploading.pause() and Paused.resume() transitions; Queued and Done untouched. Network-drop is an event onNetworkLost handled by Uploading (-> Paused) and ignored elsewhere.

Languages: Java, Kotlin

Languages: Java · Kotlin
class Paused implements UploadState {
    final long offset;
    Paused(long o) { offset = o; }
    public UploadState resume(Upload u) { u.startFrom(offset); return new Uploading(offset); }
    public UploadState cancel(Upload u) { return new Failed("cancelled"); }
}
class Paused(val offset: Long) : UploadState {
    override fun resume(u: Upload): UploadState { u.startFrom(offset); return Uploading(offset) }
    override fun cancel(u: Upload): UploadState = Failed("cancelled")
}
  1. Risks: race between pause tap and completion (Done arrives after Paused); stale offset; user pause vs system pause must not auto-resume the user's pause.
  2. Fix for the last: two reasons in Paused (USER, NETWORK); only NETWORK auto-resumes.
  3. Prevention: transition tests including "pause while finishing".
  4. Trade-offs: a boolean flag would be quicker but would spread if (paused) through every method.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Persist across process death? -> Store state id and offset in a DB.
  • Metrics? -> Count transitions per state.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: Auto-resume overrode explicit user pauses until the reason was modelled.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: boolean flag.
  • Hire: new state and transitions.
  • Strong hire: races, reason modelling, persistence.

questions.contextHtml: A teammate proposes State classes (Loading, Loaded, Error) with a context and factory for a screen that has three display modes and no transition logic beyond "request finished". In Kotlin they could use a sealed class.
questions.promptHtml: Do you accept the State-pattern version? What would you do?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Yes, patterns scale."

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Are there behaviours (methods) that differ per state, or only data to display? How many transitions exist?
  2. Decision: no. These are data states, not behaviour states. Use sealed interface UiState { Loading; Data(items); Error(msg) } and a when in the renderer.
sealed interface UiState {
    object Loading : UiState
    data class Data(val items: List<Item>) : UiState
    data class Error(val msg: String) : UiState
}
  1. When State pattern is right: behaviour per state differs and transitions have rules (order lifecycle, connection manager).
  2. Also acceptable: an enum with a transition map for 3-6 states with simple rules.
  3. Cost of the pattern: three classes plus a factory and no real polymorphic behaviour to hold.
  4. Trade-offs: sealed + when gives exhaustiveness checks, which is the main benefit.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Rules grow later? -> Refactor then; cheap and local.
  • Java 17? -> sealed interface and switch patterns.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A UI state hierarchy with empty methods got deleted for a sealed class, removing 200 lines.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: accepts by default.
  • Hire: data vs behaviour distinction.
  • Strong hire: sealed exhaustiveness and clear threshold for switching.

questions.contextHtml: A text editor with 50 MB documents needs undo/redo and macro recording. Typing 100 characters creates 100 commands; the history grows to 1.2 GB after a long session; users complain that Ctrl+Z removes one letter at a time and redo vanishes after they undo twice and type.
questions.promptHtml: Fix memory, UX, and the redo bug.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Snapshot the whole document per keystroke.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Required history depth? Collaborative editing (operational transform) needed? Are formatting and text changes one history?
  2. Immediate mitigation: cap history at N=200 commands.
  3. Approach: commands store deltas (Insert(pos, text), Delete(pos, removedText)), not documents.
  4. Coalescing: merge consecutive inserts adjacent in position and within 1s into one command via mergeWith(next).
  5. Redo rule: a new command clears the redo stack; that is correct semantics, not a bug, unless the user expects a branching history (tree undo).

Languages: Java, Kotlin

Languages: Java · Kotlin
interface Cmd { void execute(); void undo(); boolean mergeWith(Cmd next); }
void run(Cmd c) {
    c.execute(); redo.clear();
    if (!undo.isEmpty() && undo.peek().mergeWith(c)) return;   // coalesce
    undo.push(c);
    if (undo.size() > MAX) undo.removeLast();
}
fun run(c: Cmd) {
    c.execute(); redo.clear()
    if (undo.lastOrNull()?.mergeWith(c) == true) return
    undo.addLast(c)
    if (undo.size > MAX) undo.removeFirst()
}
  1. Macros: a CompositeCommand holding children; undo runs children in reverse.
  2. Prevention: tests: type 100 chars undo once -> all gone; undo, type, redo disabled.
  3. Trade-offs: coalescing windows are a UX choice; a rope or piece-table document makes deltas cheap.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Undo across saved checkpoints? -> Mark the save index in history.
  • Collaboration? -> OT/CRDT; local undo becomes inverse of own ops only.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: Snapshot-based undo worked in demos and failed at 20 MB files; delta commands cut memory by three orders of magnitude.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: snapshots.
  • Hire: delta commands, bounded history, coalescing.
  • Strong hire: composite macros, redo semantics, collaboration limits.

questions.contextHtml:
Orders are cancelled by customers and shipped by the warehouse service concurrently. Production: 0.2% of orders end up "SHIPPED" and refunded. Log excerpt:

12:00:01.120 order=991 cancel() state=PAID -> CANCELLED refund issued
12:00:01.123 order=991 ship()   state=PAID -> SHIPPED   label printed

The state is a field read then written without synchronisation across two services' threads.
questions.promptHtml: Explain and fix the race at the code and database level.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Make the method synchronized; ignores multiple instances/services.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: One JVM or many? Is the state persisted in a DB? Are side effects (refund, label) idempotent?
  2. Immediate mitigation: reconcile bad orders; pause auto-ship for cancelled flags.
  3. Root cause: check-then-act on the state: both threads read PAID, both transition, and side effects fire for both.
  4. Fix: make the transition atomic where the state lives. In a DB: conditional update.
UPDATE orders SET status='CANCELLED', version=version+1
WHERE id=991 AND status='PAID';   -- rows affected 0 => lost the race, do nothing

Do the side effect only if the update returned 1 row; use an outbox for the refund event.

Languages: Java, Kotlin

Languages: Java · Kotlin
boolean cancel(long id) {
    return jdbc.update("UPDATE orders SET status='CANCELLED' WHERE id=? AND status='PAID'", id) == 1;
}
fun cancel(id: Long): Boolean =
    jdbc.update("UPDATE orders SET status='CANCELLED' WHERE id=? AND status='PAID'", id) == 1
  1. In-memory only: AtomicReference.compareAndSet(expected, next) instead of a plain field.
  2. Prevention: concurrent test firing cancel and ship; invariant check "never SHIPPED and REFUNDED".
  3. Trade-offs: optimistic update (fast, retries) versus row lock SELECT ... FOR UPDATE (simpler, contention). A synchronized method alone does not help across instances.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Ship won, cancel loses? -> Return a clear "too late" response, offer a return flow.
  • Idempotent refund? -> Refund keyed by order id.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: Two services each "validated" the state and both acted; a conditional update plus outbox ended the double actions.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: synchronized.
  • Hire: conditional update/CAS.
  • Strong hire: side-effect gating, outbox, tests and trade-offs.

questions.contextHtml: A mobile app queues UploadPhoto commands (offline-first) and replays when online. After a connectivity flap, support sees duplicate posts: queue shows UploadPhoto#771 executed 3 times. Logs: POST /photos 200 (client timeout 10s) x3. Commands capture a Bitmap and the user's current albumId via a shared mutable Session object; some uploaded photos landed in the wrong album.
questions.promptHtml: Diagnose both problems and redesign the commands.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Increase the timeout.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Does the server dedupe? Is the queue persisted? How long can a command wait?
  2. Immediate mitigation: server-side dedupe window by key; disable auto-retry on timeouts for POST.
  3. Hypotheses: timeout with a successful server write followed by retry (non-idempotent command); commands read mutable shared state at execute time (stale album).
  4. Verify: server logs show 3 requests with the same photo hash; queue records show album id mismatch.
  5. Root cause: commands are not self-contained and not idempotent.
  6. Fix: capture all inputs at creation (immutable values, file path not Bitmap); attach an idempotency key.

Languages: Java, Kotlin

Languages: Java · Kotlin
record UploadPhoto(String id, String filePath, String albumId) implements Command {
    public void execute(Api api) { api.upload(filePath, albumId, /*Idempotency-Key*/ id); }
}
data class UploadPhoto(val id: String, val filePath: String, val albumId: String) : Command {
    override suspend fun execute(api: Api) = api.upload(filePath, albumId, idempotencyKey = id)
}
  1. Queue: persisted (Room/WorkManager), bounded retries with backoff, dead-letter after N failures.
  2. Prevention: tests that replay the same command twice; code review rule: no references to mutable session state inside commands.
  3. Trade-offs: persisting commands needs a stable serialisable schema and version handling.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Order of commands matters? -> Per-entity serial queues.
  • App updated with old queued commands? -> Version the command schema.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A queue replay after a tunnel posted every photo three times; idempotency keys turned the incident into a non-event.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: bigger timeout.
  • Hire: idempotency and captured inputs.
  • Strong hire: persistence, dead-letter, schema versioning.

questions.contextHtml: A drawing tool has MacroCommand (a list of commands) with undo. Users report that undoing a failed macro leaves shapes half-created: step 3 of 5 throws, steps 1-2 stay. Tests exist only for single commands and use a real canvas that needs a GPU.
questions.promptHtml: Fix macro semantics and describe a test strategy without the canvas.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Catch the exception and ignore it.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Should a macro be atomic (all or nothing)? Are commands guaranteed to be invertible?
  2. Root cause: the macro executes children sequentially without compensation on failure.
  3. Fix: on failure at index i, undo children i-1..0 in reverse, then rethrow; mark the macro not pushed to history.

Languages: Java, Kotlin

Languages: Java · Kotlin
public void execute() {
    int done = 0;
    try { for (Cmd c : cmds) { c.execute(); done++; } }
    catch (RuntimeException ex) {
        for (int i = done - 1; i >= 0; i--) cmds.get(i).undo();
        throw ex;
    }
}
public void undo() { for (int i = cmds.size() - 1; i >= 0; i--) cmds.get(i).undo(); }
override fun execute() {
    var done = 0
    try { cmds.forEach { it.execute(); done++ } }
    catch (e: RuntimeException) { for (i in done - 1 downTo 0) cmds[i].undo(); throw e }
}
override fun undo() { cmds.asReversed().forEach { it.undo() } }
  1. Test seam: commands depend on a Canvas interface; tests use an in-memory fake that records shapes.
  2. Tests: (a) execute then undo restores an empty canvas; (b) a throwing child leaves canvas unchanged; (c) undo order is reverse; (d) redo clears on new command; (e) a table-driven test for state transitions if the tool has modes.
  3. Prevention: property-based test: random command sequences, undo all, canvas equals initial.
  4. Trade-offs: best-effort undo can fail itself; for critical flows prefer snapshots/transactions over inverses.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Undo itself throws? -> Log, and stop; mark history as corrupted and offer snapshot restore.
  • Nested macros? -> Composite works recursively with the same rule.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A random-sequence undo test found a command that was not truly invertible after months in production.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: swallows exception.
  • Hire: reverse compensation and fake canvas.
  • Strong hire: atomic semantics, property test, undo-failure policy.
